utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Case IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, before I give you an opportunity to continue the examination-in-chief of the witness, I'd like to briefly address you, Mr. Krajisnik. Yesterday you asked for -- you at least suggested that a meeting would take place between at least Mr. Harhoff and representatives of the Registry. It was not entirely clear what that meeting would be about. If you would be in a position just to write down four, five, or six small points that would be on the agenda, that would be appreciated by those who might attend such a meeting. So you're invited to do that. At the same time, if financial issues would be among the items on the agenda, I am informed that, still today, that it's likely that a letter will be filed on matters related to financial aspects of being represented by counsel, representing yourself, et cetera. So therefore, if that would be one of the issues, perhaps you -- it's -- I think it's good that you're informed that something in that respect is to be expected soon. And I am informed about it because, as you may have noticed, I invited the Registry to keep me informed on -- at least to keep the Chamber informed on any information to be provided to you in relation to financial matters that are linked to assignment or non-assignment of counsel. So you're invited to draft at least an agenda so that everyone is better in a position to see whether one could follow your suggestion, yes or no. Then, Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue examination-in- chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Nielsen into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, at the conclusion of yesterday's proceedings, you were addressing the document found at tab 2 of binder 1. Before leaving that document, I'd like to ask you a couple of quick questions about that. Before I do, I'd like to indicate to the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. We had a technical problem Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I just wanted to indicate that we may not necessarily be moving through the binders sequentially, so that there would be references to different binders at different times, so that all three binders -- it would be helpful to have all three binders at your disposal as we go through the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you had indicated that the document at tab 2 enumerated certain steps which might be undertaken -- which culminated with the establishment of a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs at the republican level. Before we leave that document, let me ask you if the document also indicates whether, whatever variant was -- or option was adopted, there was some preliminary work, which should nevertheless be done.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer the question, if I may have the B/C/S copy of the document because I am used to working off of the B/C/S copy of all of these documents. Thank you. As I indicated yesterday, this document that we are looking at in -- I believe it's tab 2, does indeed enumerate several different options for decentralising Internal Affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I mentioned yesterday that there were two tiers contemplated in this document. The main question that basically underlies this entire document is, in fact, in what manner the Internal Affairs organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina can provide for full security of the Serbian population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was a particular point of concern for the Serbs in MUP and, of course, for the SDS in the second half of 1991 and early 1992, with respect to municipalities in which the Serbs were a minority. What is considered here are essentially two options, and I will later proceed to discuss in respect of other documents how this was actually done. With respect to municipalities in which the Serbs were a majority of the population in the municipality, the assumption in this particular document is that the Serbs would be able to control the public security station. I would like to state at this point that the public security station was, according to the law in place at the time, the main organ of the internal affairs organs in -- at the municipal level. However, this left the problem from -- again, from the Serbian perspective and from the perspective of the authors of this document, about what to do in municipalities in which the Serbs were a minority. In this particular case, they begin to contemplate ways in which the Serbs could either form SJBs, that is to say, public security stations - that is the B/C/S acronym for public security stations - in which they could take control and provide for security in part of the municipality in which they would conceivably then constitute a majority specifically within a part of the municipality even though they were, in fact, a minority, demographically speaking, at the level of the entire municipality. The other things that are contemplated here are a coordination with the Serbian autonomous districts that begin to exist as of September 1991. With respect to these autonomous districts, the Serbs believed that the regional organs of security and internal affairs at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina – that is to say, the CSBs, the security services centres - could be aligned particularly in areas where the Serbs were a majority with the SAOs, and indeed the documents that I've examined do tend to show that they proceeded to associate the CSBs with the SAOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, that discussion of the document can be found at the bottom half of page 5 of the English translation. If I could ask you, Mr. Nielsen, to move to tab 3 of binder 1, to a document entitled "Possibilities of organising a Serbian Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, might it be -- might I ask whether or not all the binders could be placed before the witness so he can have them at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that that would be a very practical way of dealing with the matter. Then he has B/C/S and English versions available.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have a problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It seems imminently sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can proceed meanwhile, Mr. Nielsen. Does this document go on to discuss the last option addressed in the document at tab 2, that is, the formation of a Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. These two documents are, from an analytical point of view, quite similar. Indeed, it seems very probable that whoever the drafters or authors of this document in tab 4 are, that they have read and given a lot of thought to the options that were laid out in the document that we saw in tab 2. I'm sorry, I misspoke. I meant to say tab 3, rather than tab 4. The second document here, the one we're now looking at in tab 3, is dated 17 October 1991. Like the document in tab 2, it is a document that is anonymous; that is to say, there's nothing in the document or on the document that informs us who the authors are. However, as is the case with the previous document, the document is written from the perspective of someone who is intimately familiar with the functionings of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the focus of the document is, once again, mainly the security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the operation of the Ministry of Internal Affairs from a Serbian perspective. The document here basically takes as its point of departure the assumption that it is now unnecessary to contemplate the establishment of a separate Serbian Ministry for Internal Affairs, as the title, of course, suggests. Therefore, it actually takes as its part of departure the second set, as I detailed in paragraph 37 of my report -- the second and more drastic set of conclusions from the previous document. I lay out in paragraph 40 in my report the four alternative ways in which the authors of the document in tab 3 contemplate creating or organising, as they put it, a Serbian Ministry for Internal Affairs. There is one or two points that I would like to specifically draw the Court's attention to here. Most prominently in paragraph -- in the first point that I lay out in paragraph 40, the authors are referring to the Assembly of the Serbian People and the Serbian government. As of the date of this document, that is, the 17th of October, 1991, a Serbian government had not yet been established by the Assembly, so in that way it is anticipatory of events that would follow after this date. You can group the four steps or alternatives contemplated in this document into two groups. The first two alternatives that you see on page 20 of my report in paragraph 40 are solutions or alternatives that would essentially establish a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but would allow it to cooperate to some certain extent with the existing Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Internal Affairs. This contrasts with the last two alternatives that are contemplated in this document which are, in fact, based or would lead to the establishment of a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs that would more or less be independent and would not at all cooperate or act together with the existing Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, does your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is the place where it was discovered a place that could provide us with indications about the origin?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises but did not hear the beginning of Judge Hanoteau's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll repeat the question. You said that this document was a completely anonymous one, and it was difficult to identify the person who drafted it. My question is as follows: If one is aware of the place where this document was discovered, could one draw the conclusion that such-and-such an institution or such- and-such a person had, in fact, drafted the document? Do you know where this document was, in fact, found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell the Court that, based on the ERN of this document, I recognise this document as a part of what we in OTP have referred to as the Sarajevo collection. This collection was recovered previous to my arrival at OTP, and I'm not familiar with the exact details under which it was collected. But I do know that it was collected from primarily SDS offices that had been vacated when Sarajevo was integrated, and I believe these documents were recovered first by the Bosnian authorities and then later provided to OTP. To more fully answer the question and because these two documents are, I believe, very closely related, I would like to inform the Court that in the case of the anonymous document that we already saw in tab 2, I personally was the person who gathered that document and brought it to OTP, and that document I recovered from a binder located in the headquarters of the RS intelligence services -- civilian intelligence services in Banja Luka in 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you referred to the latter two options discussed in the document at tab 3, that is, the steps that proposed -- or the options that proposed independent steps. Were unilateral or independent preparatory steps towards the establishment of a Serbian MUP taken by Bosnian Serb police officials in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such steps were taken, and my report details several such steps. It should also be stated that the thoughts, the contemplations, if you will, with respect to the organs of internal affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina that we see in both documents that we have examined are quite consistent with the conversations of leading Serbs in SR BiH MUP with SDS officials during the same period, in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I turn your attention, then, to several of the tabs and ask if those indeed reflect some of those preparatory steps. First, beginning with tab 4 at binder 1. And before I direct your -- before directing your attention to the fourth paragraph of that document and any other paragraph you consider significant with respect to this issue, can you tell the Court quickly what this document is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a document produced by the Serbian public security station at Ilidza - that is a part of Sarajevo - in September 1993. And the purpose of the document is to provide a justification for nominations for commendations for high orders, that is to say, awards, medals, by the RS for functionaries of the Ministry -- of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs. And that is also, indeed, the purpose of the subsequent couple of -- of tabs that also stem from 1993. These documents discuss, as we see in paragraph 4 of tab 4, on the first page, actions that the authors of these documents describe as "illegal." These are retrospective documents which look at the actions and dealings of Serbian members of the RS MUP, of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the RS, at times in 1991 and early 1992 at which they were still employees of the -- of SR BiH MUP. Some of the actions referred to in this document are illegal meetings conducted by Tomislav Kovac, who was at the time, as the document states, the commander of the police at the Ilidza Public Security Station. Kovac is commended in this document for having organised "illegal" meetings that helped organise the work of the Serbs within Ilidza and therefore provide the foundation for the later establishment of an exclusively Serbian police station, public security station, in Ilidza. Indeed Kovac would, once the war commenced in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Kovac would become the chief of the public security station. And as we shall see later, Kovac eventually became the assistant minister for the police within the Ministry of Internal Affairs for the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition to his commendation for organising illegal meetings, does the document also commend him for arming the Serb people or arming of Serbian people? And specifically I would refer you to page 4 of the English translation, under the enumeration 1, with his name beside it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. As we do see on page 4, Kovac is commended for what Again, and I must stress this, the authors of the documents, who are Serbian police officers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, themselves term "illegal work and arming of the Serbian people." This commendation for Kovac, as one can see on page 4 and page 5 of the document, includes commendations for other police officers besides Kovac. And we see in this particular document and in others like it the mention of illegal meetings, illegal arming of the Serbian population, often in coordination with the Serbian Democratic Party. And these documents are also consistent with the draft annual report of the RS MUP for 1992 in which it was retrospectively observed that the -- that Serbian police officers in the second half of 1991 and the early months of 1992 participated in, again, to use the words of RS MUP, "the illegal arming of Serbs in SDS municipalities".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you mentioned other police officers. If I could ask you to turn to tab 7, which is an undated commendation for Sreto Samardzija, which also mentions some activities in connection with Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sreto Samardzija, as we see in this document, was another police officer who worked under the direction of Tomislav Kovac, also referred to as Tomo Kovac, in Ilidza in 1991 and 1992. If we look at the - - in the B/C/S it's the third paragraph of the commendation for Mr. Samardzija. It says that: "Together with his commander, Tomislav Kovac, Sreto Samardzija helped to arm the Serb nation or respectively to secure places where weapons could be distributed to the Serb people in Ilidza."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And does the document also indicate further on that he coordinated tasks with the commander of the Nedzarici barracks?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Further on in the commendation, it describes an incident at a butcher shop in Ilidza. And if you could indicate quickly what that is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That incident is described on page 2 of the translation -- of the B/C/S original, that is, at the top of page 3 of the English version. This describes a single incident in approximately March 1992 when a Serb came into the -- a butcher shop, a Muslim-owned butcher shop in Ilidza, and raised a pistol, then stated that "This is a Serbian Ilidza," and began to shoot his weapon. What the document tells us is that in connection with Tomo Kovac or in agreement, rather, with Tomo Kovac, this person was found and was concealed at a hotel so that he would avoid arrest. This is quite significant, because at the time, as I have already told the Court, Tomo Kovac was the commander of the public security station in Ilidza. That would essentially be the number two position in a public security station. His superior at the time, Edin Milivic is mentioned on this page. Edin Milivic, who was a Muslim, was at the time the chief of the public security station and had ordered his subordinates to apprehend and arrest Vlastimir Jokovic, the Serb who had committed this act. Tomislav Kovac, despite being legally subordinate to Milivic, is here stated to have aided and abetted the concealment of -- or evasion of this particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, does the commendation, among other things, indicate that Mr. Samardzija took part in the disarming of what are called Green Berets and the confiscation of 32 rifles and 2 police Land Rovers?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what -- what happened to those items or what was done with those items once confiscated.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, Tomislav Kovac and Samardzija participated in an inspection of a particular Muslim settlement, and in the course of -- of that inspection, they disarmed persons that are referred to as Green Berets, Muslim paramilitaries, at the intersection of two streets in Ilidza. On that occasion, they confiscated 32 rifles, 2 Land Rovers that -- belonging to the police, and then they proceeded to hand over the same confiscated materials to Serb members of the police and members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I ask you to turn quickly to tab 10, the report on the work of the Prijedor Public Security Station during the last nine months of 1992, and ask whether if in the first -- whether the first paragraph of that document also indicates preparatory steps taken toward the establishment of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, which is the -- essentially the annual report for the public security station in Prijedor, refers here in the first paragraph to "work undertaken covertly during the months prior to the outbreak of armed hostilities in the municipality." This particular paragraph refers specifically to the establishment of what are called shadow police stations and to covert arming and equipping of the personnel with assistance or provision of arms specifically from the army, among other sources. These weapons would usually be kept by the Serbian members of the police at their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Binder 3 contains tab 63 - and I'd ask you to turn to that, please - which is a CSB Trebinje report on the work of CSB Trebinje for the period of April to December 1992. And do we see reflected in that document further steps toward the establishment of a separate Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do. CSB Trebinje, that is, the Security Services Centre at Trebinje, is an important example in understanding the establishment and operation of RS MUP. In -- prior to April 1992, there was no Security Services Centre at Trebinje, and indeed, if one consults the documents that we've already seen in binder, in tabs 2 and 3, one of the points mentioned there is the desire to establish a Security Services Centre at Trebinje in order to provide better security for the population, in particular, the Serbian population of Eastern Herzegovina. Prior to April 1992, Trebinje was only a public security station, an SJB, and was subordinate to the CSB, the Security Services Centre, located in Mostar. What we see here at -- on the very first page of this document, which, like the Prijedor document, is, in effect, an annual report on the work of the CSB for 1992, is a retrospective look at what happened before. We know from this document, and also from the draft annual report for the ministry as a whole, that with the formation of the Serbian Autonomous District of Herzegovina, SAO Herzegovina, in the late summer of 1991, that a coordination was made between the Serbs working in Eastern Herzegovina in the MUP and the SDS-dominated SAO Herzegovina. In fact, the chief of -- the man who would become the chief of CSB Trebinje, Krsto Savic, referred to himself as the Minister of Internal Affairs of SAO Herzegovina. Here in this document, there's reference to the dispatching of a special unit of -- formed from the Serbian police of SJBs from all over Eastern Herzegovina to fight on the Dubrovnik front together with the JNA at the time. What is stated more fully in the draft annual report of RS MUP for 1992 is that this action in September -- September and October of 1991 took place unilaterally; that is to say, there was no attempt or any communication from Trebinje to their superiors at the time in Sarajevo concerning the dispatching of an armed unit of Serbian police to the Dubrovnik front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does the document also indicate that, in the third paragraph in the English at page 1, that "In this period, the work of Muslim staff and SJB was blocked, and orders by the official MUP in Sarajevo were disregarded in preparation for a final cessation from the BH MUP. Along this were speedy preparations for a newly organised Serbian ministry and the formation of a CSB with its seat in Trebinje"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The document does state that. And that, in fact, corroborates the information that we've also seen in the previous documents that referred to Ilidza, where Mr. Kovac was praised in the nominations for commendation for systematically reducing the number of police officers of Muslim nationality in Ilidza prior to the war so that, to quote the document, "the war began with only Serbian police officers and two police officers of Croatian nationality." That is to say, by the beginning of the war, there were no police officers of Muslim nationality in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the Samardzija commendation that you discussed earlier refers to the disarming of Muslims and handing over those items to members of the SDS. Are there other documents that reflect the police connection with members of the SDS? And specifically -- well, let me just ask you to answer that question, and then I'll turn your attention to certain documents.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are other documents that make the connection between the activities of the police during the second half of 1991 - of the Serbian police specifically - during the second half of 1991 and the first four months of 1992 with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn first to page -- to tab 57, which is also found in binder 3. That's a work record for the period April through December 1992 from the Romanija Birac CSB. And if I could direct your attention to the first paragraph of the English translation at page 3, which indicates as follows: "In the SDS organisation, which is at the forefront of the action and measures for liberating the Serbian people, the organs of internal affairs were, so to speak, the first to enter the Serbian people's fight for liberation." And if you could comment on that in connection with the earlier question about the relationship between the police and the SDS during this period of time and also any other aspect of the document that is relevant to that issue.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first page of -- of the full body of this document, which is the third page of the English translation, there is the passage that was just quoted on the role of the SDS coordinating with the Serbian organs of internal affairs already during the pre-war period. There's also a passage on the same page a little bit further down in which - it's the second-to- last paragraph on the page, on the English translation - which states that "In the municipality where is the SDS was in power until the 1st of April, 1992, the way in which the public security station had previously been organised was maintained; whereas, in the newly liberated municipalities, there were various approaches to the formation of the SJB." This observation for the region of the Romanija Birac CSB, which was also known as CSB Sarajevo or CSB Serbian Sarajevo later, is an assessment of the relationship between the SDS and the Serbs in SR BiH MUP that is borne out by other reports from subordinate public security stations in the CSB Romanija Birac area, and it is also borne out by documents from other regions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as by the draft 1992 annual report for the ministry as a whole, all of which -- perhaps this would be an appropriate moment to note. All of these annual reports focus on the period from April to December 1992, given that the ministry was established in April, so in that sense they are also sometimes termed nine monthly reports. But all of these reports also include a significant retrospective component in which they describe what was done by Serbian employees of the organs of internal affairs in these regions and municipalities during the second half of 1991 and during the months from January to -- January through March of 1992. The other observation that I wish to make with respect to this particular document is that the first paragraph identifies the struggle of the -- for the liberation of the Serbian nation, and states that "The organs of internal affairs were the first to enter into that struggle of the Serbian nation for liberation." This claim is also a claim that is consistently made by -- or in the documents of RS MUP, and it is a claim that figures prominently, as well, in the draft annual report of the ministry as a whole for 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in this respect, Mr. Nielsen. If you say that in the municipalities where the SDS was in power until the 1st of April, you seem to assign quite a lot of importance to that language. If I would say that in Country X the Socialist Party would be in power, would that mean that they were in the position to form a government or that really the party, rather than the government, would exercise power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in referring to that language, specifically the language -- the phrase "municipalities where the SDS was in power," I am merely using the exact term that is used by the Bosnian Serbs themselves in their draft annual report. What was the case, legally speaking, in the second half of 1991 and the early part of 1992 was that there was but one law on internal affairs at the republican level. That was a law that had been enacted in 1990, and, of course, all police officers in all municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were bound by that law, regardless of which ethnicity or -- ethnicity, nationality, or party affiliation for that matter they identified themselves with. What emerges from the annual reports compiled by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the RS - and these are, of course, reports that are compiled either at the very end of 1992 or at the outset of 1993 - is that there were actions taken according to them during this period in -- that is to say, before the establishment of an RS Ministry of Internal Affairs, that were particular to municipalities in which the SDS controlled. And these activities, roughly speaking, are the activities that are contemplated in the -- not only the documents in tabs 2 and 3 on the possibilities of organising a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs, but also later in the 19 December instructions distributed by the SDS in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, can I ask you to turn next to tab 77 in binder 3, which contains a report on the work of the Zvornik SJB for the year 1992. If I could direct your attention to page 14 of that document, the second paragraph after the heading "Measures and activities which were aimed at the creating and functioning of the Republika Srpska MUP and data on personnel." Does that indicate preparatory steps that were taken in the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. This particular page indicates that a small group of employees - actually, the initial group is a group of six employees of Serbian nationality of the public security station in Zvornik – was, according to this document, in permanent contact with the steering committee of the SDS. Now, that group of six persons we see later in the document is then expanded, that is to say, more persons are recruited into this group so as to proceed with the implementation of the plans initially conceived by that group in coordination with the SDS steering board at the municipal level. This, once again, is a point at the municipal level here in this document, particularly for SJB Zvornik, that is stated in the RS MUP draft annual report at a macro level, that is to say, at the level of the RS as a whole, where it's -- where the draft annual report for the ministry informs us that smaller groups of Serb employees initially worked to recruit other members of Serbian nationality before the war in order to prepare for the creation of a separate and Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Following the statement in the report that the initial group of SJB employees was in permanent contact with the steering committee of the SDS with the aim to prepare for detachment of the SJB, does it indicate that, on the basis of received instructions, this group of employees gathered support and prepared other SJB personnel of Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn back now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in this respect. The steering committee of the SDS, do you have any information on the level on which this steering committee operated? What was that, on the municipal level? Was that on the regional level? Was that on the republican level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will just take a small moment to consult the B/C/S here. In the B/C/S original - and this is a fact that I believe is incorrectly reflected in the translation - the B/C/S original refers to the "glavnim odborom stranke SDS," the Main Board of the SDS party. Generally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please guide us to the relevance B/C/S page. Is that 084, last three digits? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you, then, please tell us approximately where we find it and read it slowly so that we'll receive proper translation of the specific portion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The B/C/S portion -- I will just read the sentence. It is after the A, lower case A, at the beginning of the paragraph. It is the - first, second, third - third line, starting with the three-letter word Vec, V-e-c.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Already."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please read that in B/C/S slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] "Already by the beginning of January 1992, a group of six workers from the police station started to have permanent contacts with the main committee of the SDS party with the aim to prepare the separation of the police station in case a division came about, that is to say, a division of the territory of the municipality into a Serb and a Muslim part of the municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, Mr. Tieger, we very often have heard about the Main Board of the SDS. Is that something, in the view of the Prosecution, something different from the Main Committee, or is that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I am familiar with the fact that the same words have been translated in a different manner. Of course, I'm familiar with that in English; Mr. Nielsen is familiar with it in -- in both B/C/S and English. His original translation was "Main Board." I would have to check the documents in which the "Main Board" about which the Court is inquiring has a corresponding B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to see if it corresponds directly with this. But I think Mr. Nielsen can probably answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note "board" would be correct, as well. We just did not have the official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nielsen, from what you know, what is presented often to this Chamber as the Main Board of the SDS, which was an organ of the SDS, as far as I understood, in which leading persons of municipalities would Meet. Is that, in your view, is it the same organ we are talking about, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not an expert on the internal workings of the SDS party, however, I would like to observe that, as Your Honour will be able to see, that in the particular B/C/S portion that I just read, the word "Glavnim," "Main," is capitalised, which is usually done to refer to a proper noun -- a proper and recognised body, as opposed to any main board. This would have the connotation of being the Main Board of the SDS. I can only speculate, but it is possible, if not probable, that this particular reference, given the use of the capital "G," is a referral to the Main Board to which Your Honour refers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Although I do understand that it's speculation. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I'd like to turn your attention to two more documents in connection with the police view of its relationship with the SDS during the preparatory period and onward, first to tab 6 at binder 1. As I believe you indicated earlier, this is another commendation-related document, this time from the -- the station at the Blazuj. And if I could turn your attention in particular to a couple of excerpts. First of all, if you'd see in the document, there's further reference to Tomo Kovac as one of the personalities in the succession of illegal preparations for defence against what is called the restoration of Islam and subjecting of the Serb people. But further down, it refers to the SDS. And if you could indicate to us whether those references that occur under the heading "Serb Public Security Station of the Blazuj reserve militia," illuminate further the police view of its relationship with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The section of this document refers -- that I was just directed to refers to the Serb Public Security Station and the Blazuj Serb militia. The first mention that Blazuj is a constituent part of Ilidza municipality and therefore was subordinate to the public security station at Ilidza, and this is from the same series of -- of commendations that we examined a little bit earlier. Once again, the person in the centre of focus here is Tomislav or Tomo Kovac, who at the time of the pre-war station was the commander of the public security station in Ilidza. According to this document, his arrival to the post of commander in Ilidza signified a turning point in the organisation of the Serbs working in Ilidza and at Blazuj. He played a very strong leadership role, and according to this document he coordinated his work and the work of the police in the -- of the Serbian police in Ilidza and at Blazuj with the president of the SDS from the community board at Blazuj, Osijek, and Rakovica. Those are other constituent parts of the Ilidza community -- or municipality, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition to close contacts with commanders and presidents of the SDS and local communities, does the document indicate that earlier, from the party's elections with the SDS, the station starting to be organised in accordance with the directors of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me next turn your attention, if I may, to tab 22 in the same binder, which contains a report on the analysis of work of the SJBs in 1992, that is, in the public security stations on the territory of the CSB Banja Luka. If I could turn your attention in particular to page 3 of the English translation, the fourth paragraph. Does that further illustrate the connection between the police and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we have seen in -- in a previous document, this particular police report, which is, again, an annual report on the work of municipal security stations on the territory of the security services centre of Banja Luka, confirms that there was a close identification between the SDS party and the Serbian employees of internal affairs organs, and that they shared a goal, as the document terms it, of realising the creation of a Serbian people's state.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Before we proceed further, if I might just indicate - and view of the fact that the witness has facility in both the -- the English and the B/C/S - it would be of great assistance, of course, to Mr. Krajisnik if both pages of the English and the B/C/S were given so that Mr. Krajisnik can also find the -- the relevant page efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Nielsen, that you would follow that suggestion so as to enable the accused to follow the -- or you, Mr. Tieger, if you point out certain pages. If I can assist, I will be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nielsen, your last comment was a reference, then, to the beginning of the paragraph -- the beginning of the fourth paragraph on page 3, which states: "The aforementioned indicators are sufficient illustration of the fact that the employees of internal affairs organs have realised that this is a struggle for the creation of a Serbian people's state and by adopting the SDS programme they have used all their abilities to achieve this goal, although most of them are not members of any political party."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- the paragraph to which I was referring in the -- in the B/C/S is the fourth paragraph on -- on page 2. It's labeled page 2 at the top, 03246153 of the B/C/S document, and refers to the acceptance by the majority of Serb employees of the organs of internal affairs in the area covered by CSB Banja Luka of the SDS programme - "programme" being capitalised in the original - although the largest number of these Serbian police officers were not members of any political party, formally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you to move as -- well, let's try to move as quickly as we can through the preparatory steps toward the establishment of the Serbian MUP. So let me next direct your attention to a document discussed at paragraphs 54 through 58 of your report, I believe. And it has been previously been introduced into evidence P415, the minutes of the meeting held in Banja Luka on 11 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have that with me at this moment, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The particular document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO perhaps so that we can follow at least the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, if you can tell us about the significance of this meeting and its context in the steps towards the establishment of a separate Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we have in front of us is basically the minutes of - - of a meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, 1992. The list of attendees is written at the top, and without going into the function of every person at the top of that document, they are all or were all at the time leading Serb members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of SR BiH. I may just take the quick opportunity to return to Your Honour's question, Judge Hanoteau's question, of yesterday referring to Dragan Devedlaka, where I had the opportunity to consult with my own binders of MUP documents and confirm that he was indeed a member of the State Security Service at the time of this document and at the time of the intercept that we listened to yesterday. So all of the people who we see in the list of attendees here would come to play prominent roles in the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs once that was established at the beginning of April 1992. The main purpose of this meeting, it appears from the contents of it as a whole, is to discuss the way in which a Serbian Minister -- Ministry of Internal Affairs will actually be established. This is a meeting that takes place only a few weeks before the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina pass what would become the Law On Internal Affairs for the Ministry -- for the future ministry. There's quite a lot of impatience exhibited in -- among the members of this meeting with regards to the establishment of the ministry; several of them state that the ministry should be established as quickly as possible. One of the first speakers, the second speaker on the first page, Mico Stanisic, was the person who would become the Minister of Internal Affairs of the RS. The key conclusions, as I state in my report, from this meeting relate to the creation of a so-called Serbian council board. That would be on -- the conclusions start on the fourth page of the translation and on the sixth page of the B/C/S original. This involved having a Serbian steering council within the ministry which would direct the acts of all the persons within the ministry who are of Serb nationality and, in particular, carry out the preparations necessary for the functioning of a Serbian MUP after the adoption of the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of BiH. On the first page of the document, as well, there is a reference to the Council of Ministers in the statements of Mico Stanisic. Here it says in the English - I now see the translation - "ministerial council." However, I take it, based on my review of the documents, for that to be a reference to the Council of Ministers that the Court is already familiar with. This meeting was a one-day meeting, and I'll conclude my observations on this document by noting that two days after the meeting Momcilo Mandic, who was at the time an assistant minister in the SR BiH MUP, sent a dispatch to the persons listed in paragraph 59 of my report asking them to arrange meetings with leading personnel in their areas of responsibility so as to implement the conclusions of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could perhaps the B/C/S version of this document, the relevant part, be put on the ELMO just for a second, because you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's some distance from the translation, so that at least Mr. Krajisnik is able to see whether he would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had it available on Sanction. It's on there now if that's helpful. We could try to turn to the appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- page, if that's what you had in mind. I'm advised that's where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least we can now see what it says in the original. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Nielsen, there was reference in the intercepted telephone conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Zepinic that we heard yesterday to a collegium, I believe, in the MUP. Can you just tell us quickly what that was.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference that we heard yesterday in the intercepted conversation between those two persons referred to instructions that Karadzic was giving to Zepinic as the leading or top-ranked Serbian employee at the time of the ministry to essentially ensure that the employees of the ministry -- the leading employees of the ministry who were of Serb nationality would meet daily, as it were, for coffee in the morning to discuss the most-pressing issues for employees of Serbian nationality. It is the case that Karadzic spoke very frequently, as I note in my report, with not only Vitomir Zepinic, the deputy Minister of Internal Affairs, but also with Momcilo Mandic, who was one of the assistant Ministers of Internal Affairs. There is reference in these conversations to these meetings, and this was a way in which Mr. Karadzic could make his views known and ascertain whether those views were being followed or implemented by Messrs. Zepinic and Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the document of 11 February 1992 refers to the Council of Ministers. And to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- if I just may interrupt. Could I ask you, Mr. Tieger, to come a bit closer to the microphone and you, Mr. Nielsen, to get a bit of distance from the microphone, because what happens is that you have a very clear and loud voice, so you have to adapt all the time the volume in order not to lose my hearing and for you, Mr. Tieger, to hear at all what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will move closer to the microphone and also speak more loudly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, as we saw, the minutes of the meeting of 11 February 1992 refer to the Council of Ministers' position that in the territory of SR BH, which is under Serbian power, this power has to be felt. Let me turn your attention, if I may, to another body of the Bosnian Serb authorities, and that is the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and ask you about reflections of the movement toward a separate Serbian MUP that are reflected in the Assembly in the first few months of 1992. And if I could first turn your attention to just before the break the Seventh Assembly Session, on February 15th, 1992, which is already in evidence as P65, I think binder 8, tab 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think we'll need to pull that out, Your Honour. There's a brief -- relatively brief reference that I -- to a portion of that Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You intend to read it or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me first ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How are you going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me first ask the witness if he's familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- with that session and with -- in particular, with any comments that bear on the movement toward the establishment of a separate Serbian MUP made during that session.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that session, having read the entire stenographic minutes of the session, and I do recall that several speakers at the session made comments pertaining to the police in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, just before we break, to the comments of Mr. Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'll have this put on the ELMO in just a moment, but perhaps the most efficient way is for me to read the comment and then have it put on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could do both, couldn't we? You read and we look at it when it appears on the ELMO. But this should not refrain you from starting to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour,.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Nielsen, who was Vojo Kupresanin, very quickly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojo Kupresanin was one of the leading SDS politicians from the Autonomous Region of Krajina in North-western Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that session, did Mr. Kupresanin state: "If this is a Serbian republic, can it have any other police but a Serbian police? The Serbian police should have their own insignia, they should have their own symbols and their ties with Serbian history and Serbian tradition." And then he goes on to say: "Are we Serbs? Are we going to fight for the Serbian people or for some half-baked abstract goals?" And he finally -- and he continues toward the latter part of his comments: "To achieve result, we shall have to make some choices today. Do we want a Serbian republic? Do we want a Serbian police? Do we want a Serbian army?"

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin did make these comments at the Assembly session that we are now looking at. This comment that he makes regarding the need to establish a Serbian police and, for that matter, he also refers to a Serbian army, he sees that - and this is a view that was widely held at the time by the members of the Assembly of the Serbian nation - that in forming a Serbian state, one would of necessity, in order for that state to be viable, have to form a Serbian police force and a Serbian army. If I may refer to the 19 December instructions with which I know the Court is already very familiar. The police are also identified there as one of the -- the three pillars, together with the army and the social accounting service, for any Serbian state or Serbian republic to be viable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau will have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these minutes of the Assembly, are there references to who said what? Is there anything like that? Are these minutes of the Assembly something where we have references to comments made by those present? Were there any comments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Does Your Honour wish me to comment on this particular session or on the sessions in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. First of all, I'd like you to tell me in general about the nature of these minutes. Is it just a summary, or do we have actual comments from the people who participated? Generally speaking, not with reference to this particular session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, generally speaking, these stenographic records of the Assembly do list the person who is making the comments at the time. This particular set of Assembly stenographic records actually right after Mr. Kupresanin's comments, there is a few pages later, I recall, a speaker where it specifically says "name not mentioned." It seems to have been the practice of the stenographer at the time to take his or her cue from the speaker of the Assembly, who would introduce each speaker, but it does appear that sometimes if the exchange was particularly rapid, as it I know sometimes also is in a courtroom, the stenographer would not have the opportunity to make a note of the -- of the name. In this particular case, the person who is not identified is subsequently identified by Mr. Krajisnik as being Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. My question was asked for the following reason: At that particular session on the 15th of February, were there any dissenting opinions or was there a kind of unanimity regarding this project about the Serb police, et cetera? Had anyone voiced any reservations at least, or did anyone disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not recall from this particular session any strong dissenting opinion about the formation of a Serbian police. Rather, the discussion, if one proceeds to read what is around the pages in which Mr. Kupresanin makes his comment, is a rather lengthy and detailed discussion about the exact design, heraldic design for the coat of arms for the Serbian state and the future Serbian police. There also seems to be an opinion voiced by Mr. Kupresanin himself and to the aforementioned Mr. Tosic in which Kupresanin explicitly, and Mr. Tosic explicitly as well, criticise unnamed members of the Serbian police or Serbian Assembly of behaving as "communists," or of not being sufficiently proactive in their approach to the creation of a Serbian police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on that day, the 15th of February, who chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to consult the minutes. If I may use the ELMO, I will put page 2 of the English original, which is actually the first page of the actual debate, which state that the session commenced at 10.00 in the morning and that Momcilo Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly of the Serbian People, presided over the session. And he did certainly preside over this portion of the session in which Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Tosic spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one follow-up question before we break, please. It's directly on the heels and following Judge Hanoteau's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was the speaker who followed Mr. Tosic, President Krajisnik, and he did say: "I fully agree with Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Tosic"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break. Before we adjourn, I'd like to inform everyone in this courtroom that there would be an opportunity to sit tomorrow in the morning. And since I know that it's often appreciated, especially on Fridays, to sit in the morning, I'd like to know from the parties and also from you, Mr. Nielsen, whether you would be available, whether it would be possible to sit in the morning. And if not, would you then also consider to start a bit earlier in the afternoon and to finish a bit earlier? I leave it to you. And I'd like to hear from you after the break. We'll adjourn until 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to hear from the parties their views on changing the schedule for tomorrow. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that question, I would prefer at this late stage not to change to the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And a bit earlier in the afternoon? Would that be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm not adverse to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if that would be -- well, let's say, to start at 1.00 until 6.00 would be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That would be fine by me, Your Honour. I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one further matter I might indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I was asked by Mr. Krajisnik to ask you: Your Honour mentioned previously about Mr. Krajisnik producing a document, and he just wanted to confirm that Your Honour would be expecting such a document tomorrow, rather than today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And "document" is a big word for just -- a piece of paper just indicating what -- I mean, it's not a part of the procedure. It's just to indicate what he'd like to discuss at such a meeting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, I'd like to ask you to make all the necessary arrangements to start one hour earlier tomorrow, preferably at 1.00, and then to continue until, I take it, a quarter to 6.00, which is the usual time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Court intended to ask the witness if there was any issue with respect to his schedule that might preclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course. I should have asked. So under the condition, we fully agree, Mr. Tieger, it was not correct of me to take a decision already. We'll ask him. But before we ask the witness to come in, there's another matter on my desk, and that's the decision on the fifth batch of 92 bis witnesses, which I'd like to deliver right away. This is a decision on the fifth batch of 92 bis witnesses. I'd like to ask you, Mr. Registrar, to hand out to the parties a list showing the names of the 92 bis witnesses who are not required to attend for cross- examination. I'll start already. The Chamber has already delivered decisions on two witnesses of the fifth batch. I'll now specify what the Chamber has decided in respect of each of the five remaining witnesses from the fifth batch. With respect to Witness Thornbury, the Chamber, in accordance with the submissions of both Defence and Prosecution, has no objection to the admission into evidence of the requested material; however, the documents mentioned in the annexes are not admitted into evidence. Only the authentication is relevant at this moment. As far as Witness 606 is concerned, as you'll see in the handout, only the transcripts are admitted into evidence. With regard to the statements and their addendum, the Chamber requires some clarification from the parties. The Defence has indicated that it would oppose the admission of the statement and the addendum; however, the Chamber observes that there are two statements, both signed on the 13th of October 2001. Before making its decision, the Chamber would therefore like to receive some clarification from the parties whether they are referring to one or to both statements. With respect to witness Sebire, the Chamber has followed the submissions of the Prosecution and the Defence. As shown in the handout, the Chamber has no objection to the admission of the requested evidence, which meets the 92 bis admissibility requirements. And finally, in relation to Witness Kahriman, the Chamber agrees with the Defence that there should be an opportunity to put direct questions to the witness. She deals with an unexplored area on which the Defence seeks further clarification. The Chamber therefore requires witness Kahriman, unlike the other witnesses, to appear for cross- examination. The associated material is not shown in the handout. The documents relating to this witness shall be admitted into evidence, subject to any further objections, at the time the witness is heard in cross- examination. The Chamber requires that the Prosecution submit the material admitted through this decision to, as the decision reads, "Madam "Registrar, unlike in the beginning we talked about Mr. Registrar, but we take it that Ms. Philpott will deal with the matter. And then in due course, Madam Registrar will assign exhibit numbers to those items and inform the parties and the Chamber. I kindly ask Madam Registrar - but that could also be Mr. Registrar - to file the handout under seal. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the fifth 92 bis batch. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Nielsen into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, before we continue your examination as a witness, how about your availability, especially tomorrow in the afternoon, starting a bit earlier? Would that be possible for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, I would kindly ask you to make the necessary arrangements for a start tomorrow at 1.00, rather than a quarter past 2.00. And before, Mr. Tieger, I give you an opportunity to continue the examination-in-chief, Judge Hanoteau would have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. In your statement, earlier on you referred to illegal meetings organised at Ilidza between police officers and the representatives of the SDS. If we look at paragraph 28, page 86 of your report, we can see that you say "the aforementioned illegal meetings." I would just like to try and understand why you are describing these meetings as "illegal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Judge Orie has just pointed out, in the document which has been submitted to us, the reference is to illegal meetings, as well. Why illegal? Can you give us a reason why you're describing them as illegal? Does it mean that all meetings of police officers were banned or all meetings involving members of political parties were banned or what? Could you perhaps elaborate upon that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can certainly elaborate on that; although, it would help me if Your Honour could repeat the number of the paragraph to which Your Honour is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 68, page 28 of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is, indeed, a puzzling use of the word "illegal." Let me explain. At the outset of the report, I referred to the November 1990 elections, which led the way for three essentially ethnically based parties, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, to come to power. And all of those three parties agreed that they would henceforth divide the positions in the Ministry of Internal Affairs among them. There was, therefore, no disagreement among the three parties that consultations would take place on a regular basis between the respective political representatives in those three parties and the various high-ranking members of the ministry. Whenever I use the word "illegal" in the report, as indeed is the case in paragraph 68, Your Honour will notice that I do so in quotation marks. That is to denote that I am not taking any position on the legality or illegality of such meetings. Specifically the word "illegal" is the word used by the author of that document. In this particular case, there is, based on the laws in place at the time, certainly based on the law of internal affairs and based on the customary practice at the time, nothing illegal about such a meeting; whereas, in other cases, such as distributing arms, that is also referred to as being an illegal practice, that was indeed illegal based on the laws at the time. But such meetings were, as far as I know, legal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was no ban on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. political parties bringing together civil servants in order to talk about whatever they thought they should.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such ban, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, your report deals in some detail, beginning at paragraph 73 to approximately paragraph 79, with some of the sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly during the months preceding the split of the MUP that addressed the imminent separation of the MUP and the establishment of a separate Serbian MUP. Unless there is some reason to illuminate or highlight or clarify any aspect of that, I'm going to turn your attention next to a document that appears at tab 67 in binder 3, which is an SDB report from Belgrade regarding the security situation in the area of Bihac. But I leave to you whether we can move forward without comment at this point.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see any need at this stage to comment more fully on the passages that I quote from the Assembly in the aforementioned paragraphs unless there are any specific questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in those paragraphs, among other things, you identify the comments of Miroslav Vjestica, an SDS delegate from Bosanska Krupa, whose comments from the 11th Session of the Assembly and, again, from the 12th Session of the Assembly are quoted. Does the document shown at tab 67 reflect on the situation in Krupa shortly before the splitting of the MUP and the establishment of a separate MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Let me first make a specific comment on Mr. Vjestica's interventions in the Assembly. If the Court will turn to footnote 108 on page 29 - excuse me - in my report, I refer to a comment made by Vjestica, who was a strong proponent to the creation of a Serbian police force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in which he states that People's Defence, that is to say, the army, the military, the SUP, which is the old acronym for the Secretariat for Internal Affairs at the municipal level, and the SDK are elements that need to be controlled in order to take power, as he puts it. This is -- I just wanted to make that reference because I noted earlier that those three institutions were mentioned in the Assembly as institutions that needed to be controlled if a Bosnian Serb state were to be established. The document that we have in front of us in tab 67 is a document produced outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was produced in Belgrade in March of 1992 by the State Security Service of the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs, the SSUP. The authors are familiar with the deteriorating security situation at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina and are collating and commenting on the information that they've been able to gather about that security situation. On page 7 of the English translation and on page -- well, it's also page 7, B0031446 of the B/C/S original, there is a section specifically devoted after Roman numeral III to Bosanska Krupa municipality. The authors of the document state that the municipality at that point -- they give some demographic figures, that it is 74 per cent Muslim, 24 per cent Serb, 2 per cent Yugoslav and remainder, and then go on to comment on the security situation in that municipality. In the first full paragraph in that section, which is on the following page, it states that "The situation in the territory of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa is quite tense." They refer to the establishment of a reserve police of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa, approximately 200 persons, and refer also to the organisation of other reserve and active components of the police from the territory of the municipality. What I would like to direct the Court's attention to is the second half of that paragraph in which it refers to the situation with respect to the chief of CSB Banja Luka, who was at that time Stojan Zupljanin. The persons writing this report have been in communication with Stojan Zupljanin and have been told by him that they are in a holding pattern, as it were, with respect to the activation of the decision on the adjoinment of -- of the Banja Luka region -- of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa to the Banja Luka region, that is, the region of CSB Banja Luka, and that they have been informed by Zupljanin that this decision will not be implemented and will not be, essentially, advanced upon until the law on the internal affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina takes place. What this shows is that the -- first of all, it shows that there is a Serbian police force that has been organised on the territory of Bosanska Krupa already in March of 1992, and it also shows that the police in Belgrade, the State Security Service in Belgrade, was aware that such a -- not only that such a police force existed, but that there was an implementation plan to join Bosanska Krupa police to Banja Luka. It needs to be stated that as of the writing of this report per the 1990 Law On Internal Affairs, Bosanska Krupa Municipal -- Public Security Station was subordinate not to Banja Luka, but, rather, to the CSB in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I return for a moment to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't mind, could we go back to paragraph 74 of your report. You're referring to what happened at the 11th Session of the Serb Assembly, and you say that Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Vjestica made two comments. Could you comment and tell us what was the purpose of that session, and you simply quote three words that Mr. Krajisnik had said. Could you perhaps give us a more complete analysis of what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I recall the 11th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which was held on 18 March 1992, a major topic of discussion, although many individual points were discussed, as at all Assembly sessions, was the impending establishment of a Bosnian Serb republic. If Your Honour wishes me to comment in more detail on Mr. Krajisnik's comments at that Assembly session, which I quote only briefly, I would like to have the relevant passage in -- in the B/C/S made available to me so that I can consult that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I take it that you have a copy of the 11th, or do you not have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do not have it with me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't, but my case manager does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your copy would have been as good, Ms. Loukas, as the one of the case manager, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to state, Your Honours, that since Mr. Krajisnik, as the speaker of the -- and president of the Assembly speaks on very frequent occasions throughout the session, I would appreciate it if any of the parties could guide me to the specific part of the transcript at which that exchange – or at which that comment does take place. Otherwise, it will take me some time to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would also agree if you would look at it during the next break, identify the portion relevant, perhaps read it, and then answer the question put by Judge Hanoteau. Would that be a practical solution? Yes. So then I take it that you will keep the 11th Session in your hands during the next break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I can indicate for the benefit of all concerned that it's at page 36 of the English version, where Mr. Vjestica speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I wanted to return just for a moment to a question posed a few moments ago by Judge Hanoteau about the use of the word or the phrase "illegal meetings" in those documents we looked at earlier. Now, I understood you to say that there was no prohibition about which you were aware of meetings between police officials and political officials as a general matter.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, would it be illegal, however, to plan or plot the dissolution of the existing joint MUP or the dissolution of the existing state?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, clearly the witness is not put forward by the Prosecution as some sort of legal expert. And in -- in those circumstances, I would object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not quite clear to me, Ms. Loukas, whether you say that this is a matter of common sense or that you would need legal expertise to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'll adjust the microphone. I'm saying that it is a legal question and it does require legal expertise. The question is quite specifically: "To your knowledge, would it be illegal to plan or plot the dissolution of the existing joint MUP or the dissolution of the existing state?" No, Your Honour, that's a question that calls upon not just local constitutional legal questions but also in relation to international law questions and what have you. And I would submit that the witness, who is not put forward by the Prosecution as a legal expert, and certainly the witness does not put himself forward as a legal expert, is not in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear, you say it should be an expert who answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me put the question this way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the course of your review of MUP-related documents, do you know whether or not Bosnian Serb police officials considered the dissolution of the MUP or efforts towards the dissolution of the MUP or efforts toward the dissolution of the state to be illegal?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, without taking a position on the legality or illegality of that question and of any actions undertaken by Serbian employees of SR BiH MUP prior to April 1992, I do wish to refer to paragraph 341 of my report in which I note that the RS MUP annual report, the draft annual report, described the recruitment of Serbian employees of SR BiH MUP to work on the "illegal organisation of Serbian MUP" as well as the "illegal arming of confirmed active employees for work in Serbian MUP."
