And I then go on to state that in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs had, with assistance of Serbs in SR BiH MUP - that is to say, in the period preceding April 1992 - been "illegally armed" in municipalities controlled by the SDS. In all three cases - I believe there are three cases there in which I use the word "illegal" in that paragraph - that is the term used by Bosnian Serbs who worked for RS MUP to describe their own activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you referred earlier to the Mandic dispatch of 31 March 1992, which this Court has already received in evidence as both P420 and P64 and 65, binder 11, tab 117. Was -- did that document mark the separation of the joint MUP and the establishment of the separate Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that it is correct to state that if any one single document can be identified as the document that marks the official establishment and announcement of the establishment of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, then it is indeed this document, dated 31 March 1992 and sent by Momcilo Mandic out to members of the ministry as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of your testimony, we heard an intercept between Mr. Zepinic and Dr. Karadzic, and you identified Mr. Zepinic as leading Bosnian Serb official in the joint MUP at that time. Did Mr. Zepinic, to your knowledge, share the commitment to the separation of the joint MUP and establishment of a separate Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears that already in the second half of 1991 Vitomir Zepinic, who was the Deputy Minister of the SR BiH MUP and who was the most senior or high-ranking Bosnian Serb in the ministry, began to lose the confidence of the other leading Serbs in MUP and most significantly the confidence of Radovan Karadzic, the leader of the SDS. By the end of 1991 or at the end of 1991, Zepinic, together with Mico Stanisic, the future Minister of Internal Affairs of the RS, was appointed to the Council of Ministers, to which I referred earlier. However, by the time of the formation of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs on the 1st of April, 1992, Vitomir Zepinic did not receive any post in the ministry. He was, in fact, offered a post of coordinator between the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs that I mentioned earlier in Belgrade and RS MUP, but he declined this position, and shortly thereafter he tendered resignation. The new Minister of Internal Affairs for the RS was Mico Stanisic, who remained in that position until January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to look quickly at binder -- at tabs 11 and 12 of binder 1. Do those tabs contain the resignation of Mr. Zepinic to the president of the Assembly of the Bosnian Serb Republic in tab 11 and a statement by Mr. Zepinic taken to -- or given to authorise officials of the Bosnian Serb State Security Service in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 11 is a letter signed by Vitomir Zepinic and sent on the 4th of April, 1992, to the president personally of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which he tenders his resignation. Tab 12 is a statement given by Vitomir Zepinic in August 1992 when he was detained in Kula Prison right outside Sarajevo, and it is a statement -- it is a statement that he gave to the representatives of RS MUP at that time, in which he retrospectively comments on his activities and the activities of others during that same period at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does it, at least in part, reflect efforts by him to prevent the ethnic separation of the special units of the police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit, singular, yes. In the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was only one special police unit that was controlled by the minister himself, and that -- that unit was ethnically mixed, as were all other units in SR BiH MUP. In the statement in tab 12 to which I just referred, Zepinic describes a meeting that he had with leading representatives of Serb nationality in that special unit. It's on page 3 of the English, and I'll try to locate it in the B/C/S. He describes it on page 203238739 of the B/C/S, in which he tried to persuade the members -- these were actually deputy commanders of the unit of Serb nationality. He tried to persuade them that a joint or multi-ethnic special police unit should continue to exist; however, after meeting with these persons to discuss that, he was called to two other meetings, which took place at the office of Momcilo Krajisnik, and at those meetings there were a number of leading Bosnian Serbs present, both from the political side and from the police, who very strongly persuaded Vitomir Zepinic to go back to the same police officers with whom he had spoken and essentially tell them that they needed to leave the joint special police unit and form a Bosnian Serb special police unit within the context of the new ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, let's move forward next to the functioning of the now separate and Serbian MUP, and in that connection can I ask you, please, to turn to tab 64 in binder 3, which is a record from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for taking the floor once again, but I would just like to understand what the actual role of that special police unit was. What was the purpose of that unit? Was it of fundamental importance, or was it just any old service, or was it really important, or was it because of this ethnic division -- what was the reason? Could you shed some more light on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The special police unit that existed - and as I stated, there was only one such unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period of SR BiH MUP - was essentially a paramilitary in the -- or special riot police unit that could be used to quell unrest, rioting, essentially handle tasks that were judged by the Presidency of SR BiH and by the minister himself to be too difficult for the regular police to handle. If I may be allowed, it would be roughly analogous to special police units that exist for that purpose in the Netherlands, in all Western European countries, and also in North America. However, it needs to be stated that throughout the second half of 1991 and the early part of 1992, there had been a vociferous debate within the ministry regarding the use of this unit. In particular, there were allegations that had been made by the Bosnian Serbs that the unit was being used unilaterally to carry out tasks that the minister, who was a Muslim, Alija Delimustafic, desired without proper prior discussion and agreement from the Croats and the Serbs in the ministry. So the use of the ministry -- or the use of the special police force itself was a topic of discussion, including at the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If one examines the minutes of those meetings, one sees references to what should be the procedure for authorising the use of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Zepinic in this report that you've got here, this statement, rather, that has been quoted by the Prosecution to some extent, does Mr. Zepinic explain what actually happened at Mr. Krajisnik's office in the course of that meeting, when he tried to convince him? Do we know anything else about that, how things went, what was actually said? I'd really like to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, on the page of the statement that I referred to previously does give a rather detailed account of that meeting. It is the only such account that I am aware of. I've not seen any description or mention of that meeting by other participants. Again, the context here is that Mr. Zepinic is giving a statement to representatives of the Bosnian Serb MUP, by whom he has been detained, at the end of August 1992 because he was at that point and indeed earlier, already in April, being accused of being a traitor to the Serbian nation. In the passage -- I'm not sure how much detail Your Honour wants, but in the passage that Mr. Zepinic has written about those meetings, it is interesting to note that he says that he was personally called by Momcilo Krajisnik, who asked that he come to his office to attend this meeting. When he went to Krajisnik's office, he found Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, Aleksa Buha, Franko Djeric [phoen], Miodrag Simovic, Momcilo Mandic, Mico Stanicic, and Milanko Karisik, all present there. Milanko Karisik, by the way, was himself a member; in fact, he was one of the deputy commanders of the special police unit to which I referred. And according to Mr. Zepinic, and I quote: "Upon my arrival, I was immediately attacked by all those present because of the meeting that I had held with a special unit and because the division of the special unit had been agreed earlier." And then he goes on to say -- there's a -- there's a bit of incompleteness and grammatical incorrectness in the original, but essentially he says -- he was told that the division of the special unit was now not possible if he -- because he had spoken to Vehbija [phoen] and Maric, who were two other commanders, because those persons with whom he had spoken were within the unitand given more authority and had a higher status than Dragan Vikic [phoen], whowas a Croat, and Milanko Karisik, the aforementioned Bosnian Serb. He was also told that it wasn't correct that he hadn't reported to the -- those present at the meeting about this meeting that he'd had with Vehbija and Maric, both of whom are Serbs, because essentially this was not along the lines of the agreement that had been agreed previously on splitting the unit. And then Zepinic says that: "I suggested that it would be most correct if I immediately handed my irreversible resignation to the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik." And he states that he had, in fact, offered a resignation to Momcilo Krajisnik two times before that meeting but that they had not been able to agree upon that. Again, I can keep going through the meetings, but the gist of the – of it is that it was explained to him in no uncertain terms that he had to go back to those two Serbs, Vehbija and Maric and get them to agree to the unit being divided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one short additional question to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the following: Under what circumstances was this statement given? Was Mr. Zepinic a suspect? Was he a witness, a potential witness? Was he -- and it says: "To authorised officials of the State Security Service," and then it mentions a date. It doesn't say what state, at least under those circumstances. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I would refer to paragraph 83 of my report, in which I state that already in March 1992 Momcilo Mandic, who, in fact, would become deputy minister of RS MUP, had publicly accused Vitomir Zepinic of being a traitor to the Serbian people. He did that in Javnost, which was a Serbian newspaper in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. This document here refers to the National Security Service, that it's a statement given to authorised employees of the National Security Service. At the time of the statement, there is only one such service that goes by that name in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is the RS National Security Service. One of the major changes after April 1992 was that whereas the term for the secret service of the police had previously been the State Security Service, the Bosnian Serbs in their 1992 law chose the name National Security Service to refer to their new secret police service. And I can also add that this statement is one of several statements given at the end of August 1992 by Mr. Zepinic and that these documents themselves were recovered from the archives of the RS intelligence and security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer suggests that he was suspected of being a traitor, but were there any charges brought against him? Was he in detention when he gave these statements? What -- could you ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Your Honour, he was indeed in detention at Kula Prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- outside Sarajevo, which was a facility that was controlled by the Ministry of Justice of the RS at that period of time. I'm not aware that any formal charges were filed against him; however, I can produce, if it interests the Court, a cover letter for these statements because they were subsequently forwarded for consideration of criminal charges. I'm not, however, aware that any such criminal charges were ever filed against Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, before we address or I ask you to address the record from the session of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior expert board of directors at tab 64, I wanted to return to an issue that was raised a moment ago. You had discussed the "illegal meetings" and the illegal arming of Bosnian Serbs by police officials, and a few moments ago you discussed the objections to the use of the special unit that was made by Bosnian Serb officials. Was one of those objections the use of the special unit to search for evidence of illegal arming in Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The Bosnian Serbs both in the police and in the SDS alleged frequently - this is something that appears in a variety of sources - they alleged it publicly in print media at the time, they allege it in their conversations that they have on the phone, and they certainly allege it within the ministry, and as I mentioned, at the session for -- the sessions of the CPCO, the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. They believed that this particular unit at the time was systematically engaging in unwarranted and intrusive searches of Bosnian Serb villages, that is to say, villages predominantly populated by Bosnian Serbs in the greater Sarajevo area, with the specific intent, declared intent of uncovering illegal caches of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I had indicated I wanted -- I was going to ask you to turn to tab 64 - I believe you may have that in front of you at this point - as we move forward to discuss the functioning of the Bosnian Serb MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's tab 64 in binder 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whilst Madam Registrar [sic] is finding the relevant page, I would like to apologise for having overheard earlier detention in Kula Prison because you said that five pages earlier, and I missed it. I apologise for asking it again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, can you tell us how -- what this document indicates about the functioning of the Bosnian Serb MUP shortly after the Mandic dispatch.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That document that we have in front of us in tab 64 is -- are essentially the minutes from a session of the steering council of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs held on the 14th of April, 1992. This is the first such meeting of the leading Bosnian Serbs in RS MUP that -- for which we have a set of minutes. There's a couple of quick points to note here. First of all, as is apparent on the first page of both the B/C/S and the English versions, they were meeting at the BiH MUP police academy or, as it was called, School for Internal Affairs, which was located at a place called - excuse me – Vraca immediately outside -- well, on the outskirts of Sarajevo. This particular school had been used by the old ministry but had been seized by the Bosnian Serbs on the 6th of April, 1992. It was henceforth for quite a number of weeks - I believe well into June, between April and June - used as the seat of the ministry, which is to say that in terms of controlling and commanding units of the ministry and in terms of having meetings such as the one that we see here on the 14th of April, this was the usual venue. However, we will also see references in this document to the location of certain senior members of the ministry at Pale, which was a few kilometres away. And to the best of my knowledge, during the period from April to June there were on any given day a large number of members of the ministry, including the minister himself at -- at Vraca, and also other members of the ministry present at Pale. But Vraca was universally acknowledged by everyone, including the political leaders of the Serbian Republic, as the seat of ministry. What this shows is that the ministry has started to function, and we see a variety of points being discussed, as one would expect, by the participants with respect to the functioning of the ministry. I would just note that if one is to -- were to compare the list of attendees on this particular -- at this particular meeting with the list of attendees at the 11 February meeting in Banja Luka, which we saw earlier, I think the Court will see why the 11 February meeting is indicative of who will be holding senior positions in the ministry at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, let me ask you to turn your attention to an interview with the minister himself, Mr. Stanisic, in October of 1992, which is contained at tab 78 in binder 3. Does Mr. Stanisic provide any insights into the functioning and operation of the Bosnian Serb MUP during 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In -- yes, he does. This is quite a long interview that was given in Javnost, the newspaper to which I referred earlier, by Mico Stanisic at the end of October 1992 in which he discusses extensively how the ministry had functioned between April, when it was established, and the time of the interview. And in the interview, he states that although there were problems present when the ministry was first functioned -- first established, rather, he says - and I will just try to find the passage in the - it's on page 2 of the translation, and it's the -- well, the original is a one-page interview. It may be quite difficult to read for those reading the B/C/S because it's in very small print. But he's asked a question by the journalist: "Are there any coordination problems between the organs of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in various regions and districts, or respectively, is the work of the service in these times of war completely centralised?" And he answers that "Luckily for us the Ministry of Internal Affairs has really functioned as a central organ and we have not had any kind of autonomous sentiments or desires for separation among the service" -- "and we have not felt any such sentiments among the members of the service." And he refers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. When reading it, you said that it had functioned; whereas, the official translation says "is really functioning," which, of course, is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, you are correct. It does say "is functioning as a central organ," and it is in the present tense. You are absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He then says that "At every meeting" -- the term in B/C/S is "collegium" "every meeting of my collegium" which is translated I know here as "meeting at department heads," that is what I refer to as the steering council of the ministry -- "all the assistants, undersecretaries and heads of security services centres from all areas were present. It has never once happened that we were not all present whenever the meeting was being held." So looking at this interview and looking at the previous document, this is one case in which he's stressing that -- that such meetings were an important element of the ministry's functioning. Ironically perhaps, as we see from the 14 April 1992 meeting, he himself was not present at that meeting which I believed to have been among the first such collegium meetings held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible to go back a little bit? I would rather do it now so that we do things in a chronological order. And I would just like to go back to the witness report and I'd like to ask the witness to refer to page 30, paragraphs 74, 75, 76, 77, and 78. In this report, there are references to Mr. Krajisnik, precisely at the time when this Ministry of the Interior was being set up. And I can see here on page 30 that even before the actual setting-up of the Ministry of the Interior, apparently there were discussions and debates within the Assembly in the course of the 11th Session, more specifically, and if my understanding is correct, on page 30, the first two lines read: "[In English] Mr. Krajisnik asked the deputies to think seriously before the next Assembly session about the best candidates in the regions for a Serbian MUP." [Interpretation] Since you seem to be fairly familiar with the way in which these institutions worked -- well, I must admit that I'm not all that familiar with this. If the Assembly was about to set up a new ministry, how come does the Assembly of the republic have to worry about the way in which this was to be organised, this new institution was to be organised? The Assembly sets up an institution, and at that stage it would be up to that institution, it seems to me, to take care of its own functioning afterwards. Now, why does the president of the Assembly, the speaker of the Assembly, ask its deputies to start thinking about who should be the region representatives or whatever even before the actual ministry is set up? Do you understand the gist of my question, even though it's a bit long-winded? And could you clarify the actual role of the Assembly and the role of the president of the Assembly on this specific occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do understand your question, and I will do my best to answer it. I have two observations. First, there is a legal role for the Assembly vis-a-vis each ministry, including the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And I can explain that role, but I do want to state that I don't think necessarily that the instance that we are specifically focusing on at the top of page 30 is an illustration of an exercise of the powers that I'm about to describe. What I think -- the way I read that particular instance is that Mr. Krajisnik, as a president of the Assembly, on that particular occasion was reminding the delegates who were from all of the different parts of the future Serbian republic to think seriously, as I state, and to consult, as they were doing anyway and had been doing ever since the November 1990 elections, with their municipal, local, and other boards in terms of making proposals for who should be running -- who should be appointed to which posts in the MUP. I would note that, as I do at a much earlier stage in the report,that Mr. Karadzic himself was quite fond of calling Momcilo Mandic, Vitomir Zepinic and others and stating that, for example, I have talked to a certainmember of the SDS in this or that municipality and they state that an ideal person for the new commander of police or the new chief of the public security station would be, and then they'd give a certain name. And he will then give that name on to Vitomir Zepinic or Momcilo Mandic, or others, and insist that they do their best to make sure that that particular candidate is, in fact, appointed to that position. Now, to return to the larger question. I think the appropriate point of departure is to state that the Assembly was, of course, the organ that had passed the Law on Internal Affairs that came into effect and was used by the RS MUP. This law was passed on February 28th, 1992. The law, however, was not the only legal instrument governing the relationship between the Assembly and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Other legal instruments that should be mentioned there are the Law on Government and the Law on the Ministries, that came later, and of course there is the Constitution. According to the laws - and I believe we will have the occasion to examine certain paragraphs in those laws - the Minister of Internal Affairs, like all other ministers, was appointed by the Assembly. We see a reflection of that in paragraph 79 at the 13th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly where the Assembly nominates Mico Stanisic, almost unanimously, as the Minister of Internal Affairs. Once he takes office, he, like all other ministers, remains responsible, at least as long as peacetime conditions obtain - matters will change a little bit in times of war - but in peacetime conditions, Mico Stanisic and other members of the government, as well as the Prime Minister, would be responsible to the Assembly. And their work could be and was examined, scrutinised, criticised, praised, et cetera, in the Assembly sessions, and there were often some very vocal and vociferous debates, opinionated debates, in the Assembly regarding the specifics of the work of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are close to a time for a break. I don't know whether this would be a suitable moment or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would have one last question about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the interview that you were looking at earlier, the interview of Mr. Stanisic, does he indicate whether or not his orders were obeyed during 1992? And it may be helpful to refer you back to the same section of the interview that you were looking at earlier.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to locate the appropriate section of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if it's helpful, you were referring earlier to the response to the question: "Are there any coordination problems between the organs of the Ministry of the Interior --"

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the response to the same question in which he refers to the meeting of the collegium, he states that "I want to state that we have a very responsible behaviour of the members of our service, especially with respect to any eventual non-compliance with respect to certain tasks or -- that they might undertake." But he says that "I think we are the only ministry during this period in which we have excluded certain members from our ranks, and that we did not do because they did anything that was contrary to Serb interests but, rather, because they had done certain things that were of a questionable character, which is really incompatible with membership in our service." And then he goes on to talk about the handful of cases in which that happens. However, the overall gist, and I am indeed looking again for the specific passage. Perhaps I can identify it on the break, if I'm allowed to take this with me. But I do recall that in this interview he specifically states that he did not have any problems with the enforcement of his orders and the ministry at any point during the period from April to October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just before we break - sorry, Your Honour - if you just could turn your attention to the portion of the interview immediately before the passage that begins: "I would also like to point out," the sentence before that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "In addition" -- that is, indeed, the sentence. "In addition, it has not yet happened that any order that I have given, of course, in agreement with the law, has been met with disobedience by any executors on the complete territory of the RS." It's a little bit difficult to translate the original there, but the key word, the -- the key word in that sentence is that he says that "None of the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs have ever been deaf to my orders," and, indeed, the by line at the very top of the interview, right under the title "rule of law established," is: "We want a ministry in which there could not be a single person who turns a deaf ear to the legal norms of the RS." So the gist of what he is saying is that not only has it not occurred that anyone has turned a deaf ear to the legal norms of the RS; they have, in fact, also been fully attentive with respect to the orders that he's given in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until ten minutes past 6.00, but not until after I have announced that we'll start tomorrow at 1.00 in Courtroom II. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Court had inquired earlier about the basis for Mr. Zepinic's arrest during the break. We located and copied the decision to render custody related to Mr. Zepinic's arrest, and I wanted to distribute that. I've presented it to the Defence, and Mr. Krajisnik has a copy, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, is there any objection? You want to have this in evidence, Mr. Tieger, or is it in evidence already? Which might well have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is not, Your Honour. I would have indicated if it had been. But because the Court inquired directly about it, I thought it would be helpful to produce it, and the Defence appear to have no objection to that in light of the Court's questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's precisely correct, Your Honour. In light of the Court's questions, I have no objections to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Tieger, but help me out if you can, this is to demonstrate the reason for the detention of Mr. Zepinic when he gave his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I was going to present it to the witness as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could I first ask you: This is a detention order. The aforesaid person shall be counted from 1800 hours on the 2nd of December, 1992, but the statement was given on the 27th of August, which, of course, is a bit difficult to reconcile with the reason why you present it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- yeah, I didn't mean -- and forgive me for misspeaking. This is the document that is most closely -- the document in our possession most closely related to that interview in detention that was discussed earlier. The Court asked for questions about whether or not -- about what the basis for detention was, and whether or not any charges followed. This is the best document we can produce in response to those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's an explanation a bit different from what it was, but -- well, let's just say that close to the time when he gave his statement he was detained for the reasons set out in this document. At least, if the witness would confirm that or if the document could be accepted as ... Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if a copy could be presented to the witness, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one small comment in relation to the document, if I may, Your Honours, and I've already indicated as such to the Prosecution. It does seem to be a rather poor copy of the original. I'm just wondering if it would be possible to attempt to find a better copy of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's certainly possible to attempt to find a better copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we'll be happy to do that, and hopefully we'll be successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's, then, proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I want to give you just a moment more to look that over, if you need to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready to answer any questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if you -- you're previously familiar with that document or not, but can you tell us whether or not that sheds light on the focus of basis for or reasons for or context of - and I know those are a lot of possibilities, but I'm sure you can address the appropriate one - for Mr. Zepinic's statement that was previously discussed.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is certainly not the document to which I was referring earlier when I referred to the document that I had seen forwarding his case, as it were, to other authorities or higher authorities, because that document would have come from the same ERN range as -- as the statements that -- or the statement that we were looking at earlier, as well as the other statements. And I do not recall having previously read this particular document. Despite the poor quality of the original in -- in the B/C/S, the crucial paragraph explaining the detention decision is quite legible; it's the first paragraph under "Rationale." And I can confirm that it does state -- what the translation says that it says, that is to say, that Zepinic allegedly recruited citizens of Serbian nationality to serve in formations of the enemy's military. I would note that, as I stated, Mr. Zepinic gave several statements at the end of August, on consecutive days, in fact, to the national Security Service, and they questioned him extensively on what he had been doing in enemy-controlled Sarajevo during the summer, because he had not been on the territory of -- controlled by the Serbs for most of the summer. And they also asked him questions about what he knew with respect to the Bosnian republic military, et cetera. That concludes my answer to the question. I do want to note that in the -- as requested by the Chamber, in the break I did examine the 11th Session of the Assembly, and I'm prepared to explain that statement about ethnic separation on the ground, having found it and read the passages around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you could proceed to do so, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please also have a copy of the English so that I can make reference to the Chamber to the correct pages because I only have the B/C/S references in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the only copy I have is -- I only have one copy, Your Honour. I'd like to follow it as we go through. Perhaps I can identify the relevant passages and thereby retain the only copy of the 11th Session that I have?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I have two copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the parties are perfectly able to resolve the matter so --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The only aspect of mine is that I've put -- no, I only have little sort of occasional underlinings or what have you, but nothing of any consequence, and orange Post-its on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that would not be a reason not to use it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What we see here on the very first full-text page, SA025712 of the B/C/S, and on page 3 of the English version, is that there are two items proposed by Momcilo Krajisnik in his capacity as president of the Assembly for discussion at that session of the Assembly. The first is: "Information on the last session of the conference on solutions for the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina," and the second point is: "Deputy's questions," mostly relating to the first point. After a very short introduction by the speaker and then a couple of shorter interventions, you have a long speech by Radovan Karadzic that starts on page 4 of the English translation and on page SA025714 of the B/C/S version. Having read that very quickly, again - it's been some months since I last read it - the essential point is that Dr. Karadzic, having recently returned along with others from the latest session of the ongoing conference, international conference to resolve the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina, gives all of the deputies an update about it, and it is a rather upbeat but not wholly optimistic summary that he gives. After his intervention, you then have the floor turning back to the speaker, the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, which is on page SA025725 of the B/C/S, and -- pardon me, you also have an intervention by Nikola Koljevic. But the floor eventually turns back to Momcilo Krajisnik, which is on page 12 of the English translation and, again, on page SA025725 of the B/C/S. Mr. Krajisnik states that the situation is not good and that the job is not done yet and that there is still a long way to go before their - - the goals can be realised. He then refers to the previous discussion, mostly to Mr. Karadzic's summary of what has been accomplished at the latest session of the international peace conference, and he -- but he summarised by stating that the EU, the European community at the time, or EC, rather, seems to have agreed to a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina on ethnic principles. But that is not enough, he says. And there is then a discussion of which maps -- there was some disagreement at the peace conference between the SDA and the SDS representatives about which maps would be used to actually implement that ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nonetheless, Mr. Krajisnik views this as a positive step forward, because previously, he states, the European community had very solidly been backing the SDA position and had been resisting anything that would be an ethnic separation of Bosnian- Herzegovinian territory. I won't go through all of the points in his speech, but he does state that he -- he states that "We have not budged from our position, as we've explained it in previous Assembly sessions," that he is satisfied that the – both the European Community and the SDA have realised that the Serbs have made their position clear and that they are not going to back down on the position as the Assembly has agreed to it. However, he statements that the Muslims continueto insist that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be internationally recognised and that it should be -- and he says "they want it," it, that is Bosnia and Herzegovina, "to be a state." And then comes the point that -- or part that I specifically refer to, which is on page SA0255727 of the original and -- it is on page - - at the bottom of page 13 of the English translation. And he says: "In this respect, it would be good if we could do one thing strategically, ethnic separation on the ground. This would begin to determine or to confirm the territory, and when this territory has been determined, then it remains for us to establish negotiations with the SDA and others how the actual institutions will function." So that is the particular passage from which I withdrew that reference to ethnic separation on the ground. I just want to make one very brief note that subsequently, on page 25 of the B/C/S, which is page SA025736, at a later stage, Dr. Koljevic, Professor Koljevic, who also played a very important role in the Bosnian Serb state, says that much more -- "We will be able to do much more when we have our own police." So that is, again, another important reference to the police and the necessity of creating the police for the proper functioning of a Bosnian Serb state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before you turn your attention away from the -- that particular Assembly session, Mr. Nielsen, just to round it out, and appreciating the fact that you could not include all relevant Assembly references, if I could ask you to turn your attention to page 46 of the English translation, which is shortly before the chairman proposes the conclusion, and it's Mr. Krajisnik speaking.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's on SA025776 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that in addition to the remarks that you addressed earlier, Mr. Krajisnik states: "I have realised that responsible government should be established in Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. To find the mechanisms for implementing the BH constitution, urgently form MUP, National Defence, money-transfer systems, take the Serbian territories," and then he goes on to list a number of other issues, including financing and the problem of SDK.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is reflected in the B/C/S original, and it is again another reference to the three pillars that I mentioned earlier: A military, the SDK system, the social accounting service, and the formation of a police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, turning back to your report, it addresses in quite some detail the Law on Internal Affairs and the rule book. The -- your discussion of the Law on Internal Affairs is reflected in paragraphs roughly 91 through 169 of your report. And I have to double-check to see if those are the precise references. That's correct. And on the rule book, from paragraphs 170 through 182. Because of the press of time and because of the detail in which you've discussed both of those in the report, I'm going to move on to the next phase of the functioning of the Bosnian Serb MUP, unless the Court has some specific questions about the Law on Internal Affairs or about the rule book. Perhaps before I do, is there any aspect of the rule book or the -- the purpose and nature of the rule book that requires further elucidation that is not covered in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RS rule book on internal organisation is a very long document that's over 200 pages long. And as I state at the outset of the discussion on the law on internal affairs, while the law determines the legal organisational structure of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the actual structure of the ministry and all of the kinds of rules and regulations that would pertain to the day-to-day functioning of the ministry, to obtain that, one has to turn to the rule book. It is an exhaustive document describing in detail the functioning of everybody from the minister down to the cleaning personnel in the ministry. It also discusses and explains how various units of the ministry and various departments of the ministry relate to each other, and it also moreover contemplates how many people are needed to fill various positions and what their qualifications have to be in order to be hired to those positions. So that's -- that's essentially the significance of the RS rule book. It bears mentioning that the RS MUP relied for most of 1992 on the old rule book, which is from 1990, and I actually do not know when the RS MUP rule book came into effect. We have several copies of it, but what one does see in the documents is reference repeatedly in the autumn of 1992 to the need to once and for all sit down and get the senior staff of the ministry to approve the rule book. In the meantime, they were relying on the old version. I don't think that poses much of a problem, however, for any analysis of the work of the ministry because, like the law, the rule book was an only barely modified version of the 1990 document. Indeed at the risk of generalising only slightly, one can say that most of the changes between the 1990 and 1992 laws evolve erasing the word "Socialist Republic" and replacing it with "Serbian Republic." So it is -- these are two very, very similar documents, but I do discuss the few - and they are important cases - in the section of the law where they differ. I'll just mention one right now, which is, as I already referred to earlier, that whereas there were nine Security Services Centres in the old SR BiH MUP, there were five, and at different locations to some degree, in RS MUP. And I can explain that when we get to the organisation of the ministry per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, your report addresses at paragraphs 223 through 227 reporting and communications of the Serbian MUP. In that connection, I'd like to turn first to a document that has already been produced in evidence at P529, tab 75, and also P64, P65, binder 11, tab 122. Those are the minutes of the extended meeting of the Council for National Security and the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on 22 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Registry has a problem. If you could provide a copy, because these numbers of binders are so huge that if there is no forewarning for using them, P65 will not always be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do two things: We'll provide that copy right now, and we'll also provide the Registrar with the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- exhibit we'll be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, if I could direct your attention to agenda item 4, which is headed "Conclusions and reports of the April 22nd, 1992, meeting." Does that address reports in reference to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In point 4 of the minutes here of this meeting, there are two references in points 3 and 4 to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The third point states that "The Ministers of Internal Affairs and National Defence should submit every day reports on the situation on the ground and on the establishment of possible accountability and the taking of measures." The fourth point states that "The Minister of Internal Affairs is to deliver a daily report on the security situation on the territory of SBiH." That is at that point the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the ministry take action around that time to ensure that such reports were available?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I ask you to turn to tab 43 of binder 2, which contains an order of Minister Mico Stanisic to all CSBs of 16 April 1992. And can you tell us quickly about that order, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order, in fact, anticipates the decision taken by the National Security Council several days later, so in that respect Mico Stanisic as Minister of Internal Affairs was ahead of -- or anticipating the National Security Council's decisions. He was, of course, also a member of the National Security Council. This particular document in tab 43 is an order from Mico Stanisic to the five CSBs that have been set up in the RS. Those are Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Trebinje, Bijeljina, and Doboj. And he is asking the -- or rather, ordering the chiefs of those five CSBs to forward reports on the -- on the number of -- of Serbian and non-Serbian employees who have been employed at the Ministry of the Interior -- of Internal Affairs of the Serbian republic. It is during this period that he sends a number of dispatches out between the 16th of April and the end of April, not only seeking this kind of information from the chiefs of the CSBs but, in fact, asking them to report on a daily basis in order that he may be fully aware of the security situation throughout the territory controlled by the RS or the Bosnian Serbs at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we know what was done with these reports? What did the Minister of Interior use these reports for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two uses for these reports based on -- on my analysis of them. The first use was for the ministry itself and for the minister himself personally so that they could be fully aware of the situation in the field or on the ground and what was going on in all the subordinate five Security Services Centres and that appropriate action could be taken based on that information that they had obtained. The second use of the report, which starts around this same time, is that the most important information submitted by CSB Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Trebinje, Bijeljina, and Doboj would be collated and put in a daily bulletin of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that would then be forwarded to the very top officials in the Serbian republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina so that they could, as well, be appraised of the security situation and of the ministry's activities. That report is the exact kind of report that the National Security Council is seeking at the 22nd April meeting that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you call "very top officials," who are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Prime Minister and the members of the Presidency. Again, with the obvious understanding that the composition of the Presidency varies between April and December of 1992, but it is apparent from the draft annual report to which I referred earlier that both the president of the government and the members of the Presidency at any given time were receiving these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And perhaps we could turn to tab 23 of binder 1, page 23, in connection with Judge Hanoteau's last question. And if it's helpful, Mr. Nielsen, I'm looking at the section that immediately precedes number 2, "Administrative and legal tasks," and it -- it actually falls under number 1, "Reporting and informing."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be page 23 of the English version of the document and page FI201308 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I believe Judge Hanoteau's question was, what was done with those bulletins of daily events, and does this annual report indicate in part what was done with those bulletins?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the fourth full paragraph in the English version and the second full paragraph of the B/C/S version on this page, it is stated that "In order to inform about security problems," it actually says "security problems" in the original or "the security problematic," "The president of the Presidency and the president of the government of the RS --" sorry, I'm mangling the original here because I'm translating it according to the original grammatical syntax. But the essence, as it says in the English version, is that "The president of the Presidency and the Prime Minister of the RS received these bulletins of daily events and that it estimates that about 150 issues of this bulletin were produced between April and the end of the year." It also says that in addition to this, the president of the government, that is to say, the Prime Minister, received over 90 different individual informations, that is to say, reports, and the president or members of the Presidency received 80 different informations on the security problems or security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, were some reports received by the -- by the republic level of government in response to direct requests?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case. I do want to note that this paragraph that I've just cited is footnoted, and I would like to direct everyone's attention to footnote 14 at the bottom of the page, which states that "The reports that were mentioned were mostly from the field of the SNB," which is the National Security Service and Crime. "Reports submitted to the member of the Presidency and Republika Srpska should not be added since some of them were prepared for both organs and for the officials."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in this respect: It seems, then, that -- and that did not appear from your previous answer who would receive those bulletins -- that the information given to the president of the Presidency to the members of the Presidency seem not to be exactly the same. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is correct. Upon reading this paragraph again, it is clear that from this particular report it states that "The president of the Presidency received the daily bulletins," not all of the members of the Presidency, but that the members of the Presidency did receive over 90 other reports on -- on various security issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I take it, then, that you wanted to say 80, because 90 was for the Prime Minister and 80 was for the Presidency and its members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are correct again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In connection with requests for reports, can we turn next, first quickly to a document that's already in evidence at P65, binder 12, tab 139. Those are the minutes from the government session of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on 24 May 1992. And does agenda item 2 reflect such a request?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first point of agenda item 2 states that "It has been concluded that the Ministry for Internal Affairs should prepare a complete and exhaustive information," in the original, but it is a reference to report, "on the security situation and the state of public peace and order in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that should be prepared as soon as possible." And it then goes on to state that "This report should pay specific," or "particular", rather, "attention to questions of crime, protection of state and private property of the Serb people, appearances or manifestations of war profiteering and appearances of abuses of the citizens of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as other questions which are relevant for an evaluation of the political state and attitude or conditions of the Serb nation."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to tab 59 of binder 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again ask one additional question. The issue was reporting, and it was explained to us that the Prime Minister and the president of the Presidency, and apart from that, also some reports were sent to the members of the Presidency. Now, this document deals with the government. This is a government meeting; is that correct? Which is, of course, not exactly the same forum as we discussed before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. However, I -- I do believe that in referring to the reporting to the president of the government any report that would be produced pursuant to a request of the kind we see here on the 24th of May, 1992, would be addressed by the minister who was in charge of composing that report to the president of the government, and it would then be disseminated and discussed at the government sessions. That was the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why was that not the usual practice for the president of the Presidency, receiving reports which he would have been expected to share with the members of the Presidency? Why is there a distinction in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not an expert on the functioning of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm not in a position to answer the question of whether the aforementioned daily bulletins that were given only to the president of the Presidency were shared by him with other members of the Presidency or whether they were kept to him himself. However, it is apparent from my examination of the Presidency minutes in 1992, again, with a specific eye to understanding any mentions of the police or organs of internal affairs at those sessions, that the police and their -- the problems surrounding the police, the conduct of the police, suggestions and orders that could be given to the police, were frequently discussed at Presidency sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab 59 of binder 3. That contains an order by Ministry of the Interior, Mico Stanisic, two days later, on the 26th of May, 1992 to the Security Services Centre. And does that appear to be a response to the government session of May 24th, and does it make explicit reference to a request by the government?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does appear to be a response to the previous order given by the government to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The date of the government session was, I believe, the 24th of May, that we were just looking at, and this is only two days later, the 26th of May. And they are referring -- in this case, we have the copy. The copy that I have, the B/C/S copy, is the copy that was sent to CSB Sarajevo. There were copies sent to the other four CSBs as well. And the introductory paragraph says that, "It is necessary to urgently compose information for the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that it is therefore necessary to gather information or data on the security of people and property on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And it then goes on to list what categories of information need to be -- what categories of information need to be reported upon. This certainly is a clear reference to the demand by the government for urgent information on the security of people and property on the territory of the RS. I would note that on the second page of the B/C/S original, and on page 3 of the translation, paragraph 5 or numeral V, special emphasis is given to reporting on the theft of cars from TAS at Vogosca, the TAS complex at Vogosca, and Ilidza is mentioned as well. These two questions, the theft of cars from Vogosca, the TAS complex, and the theft, or alleged theft I should say, of oil -- and there is, Your Honour, something missing from the English translation because the original B/C/S number 5 does not just say "Ilidza," it says "Ilidza" and then it says "theft of oil" in parentheses. These were two questions that were frequently discussed at the government, and they were, in fact, also discussed in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Nielsen, before we adjourn, can I direct your attention to -- or can I ask you a question about a document that's already in evidence, the minutes of the government session of 31 May 1992. And can you confirm from your own review of those minutes that they reflect that the Ministry of the Interior has informed the government about the current issues in the political and security situation in the republic, about the degree of public order and peace, and about other issues of importance for the safety in the republic?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I might just have the exhibit number in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I had done that. P65, binder 12, tab 141.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would direct your attention to agenda item 15.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, agenda item 15 certainly merits mentioning; however, I would first, proceeding by numerical order, briefly just touch upon agenda item 13, which is the decision on the problems of TAS at Vogosca. And I only want to mention this very briefly because we just saw TAS in Vogosca and the investigation of that situation mentioned by the Ministry of Internal Affairs as well. Here it is the Ministry for Economics that's also getting involved. But to turn to agenda item 15, it says that the Minister for Internal Affairs has informed the government on current questions of political security –- of the political security situation in the republic, the state of public order and peace, and other questions of interest to the security in the republic. And it states that: "On this occasion, it was stated that the government was not sufficiently informed on questions which are of significance for its work, and especially on the state at the front. It is concluded," or it was concluded,"that on all those questions the government must be informed regularly, especially through the Ministry for Defence, the Main Staff, and the Ministry for Internal Affairs in order that it can act in accordance with its rights and authorities in the composition of politics and positions, and in order to bring," or basically, "in order to decide on corresponding resolutions in its realisation." JUDGE ORIE: Mr. Tieger, I see you're looking at the clock. I do the same. We'll adjourn for the day. The parties are expected to make further oral submissions tomorrow on the issue of self-representation. We discussed that earlier this week. Mr. Stewart then had no -- well, could not respond immediately on the basis of a document he received only that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand there was a question of some English Authorities, or what have you, and some further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, the legal authorities included in the submission filed last Tuesday, I think it was, by the Prosecution. The Chamber has no preference on whether to deal with that at the beginning of the hearing or at the end of the hearing, so perhaps it's not necessary, if Mr. Stewart would deal with the matter, to be present at all times. I leave it to the parties to agree on whether the beginning or the end. The Chamber would like to hear how much time would be needed for that, and this is not a promise that the time indicated will be granted. We'll try to do it as efficiently as possible. We'll then adjourn for the day. I again thank the interpreters and the technical staff for their assistance. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, 1.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of June, 2005, at 1.00 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.06 p.m.,
